panels.title: Gateway up
panels.description: One replica by design, and the per-model endpoints were retired in Increment 3, so this is the availability of the platform's only API endpoint. A rejected scrape also reads DOWN: the ServiceMonitor authenticates with the master key, and a 401 leaves the target present and failing rather than absent.

panels.title: Backend state (router view)
panels.description: The router's view, not the pod's: 0 healthy, 1 partial outage, 2 complete outage. Set only once a request has touched a deployment and held in the gateway process, so it is legitimately blank after a gateway restart until traffic resumes.

panels.title: Requests/s (5m)
panels.description: Counters live in the gateway process and reset when it restarts. rate() absorbs the reset; a cumulative total would misreport it.

panels.title: Server errors/s (15m)
panels.description: 5xx only. 401 and 403 are the API-key check and virtual-key scoping working as designed, so they are excluded here and from the alert.

panels.title: TTFT p95 (streaming)
panels.description: STREAMING REQUESTS ONLY: LiteLLM records time-to-first-token under a stream=True guard, so non-streaming traffic leaves this blank however much of it there is. Blank also means fewer than two observations in the window, since rate() over a single sample is zero. Read this sceptically at low traffic: a percentile over a handful of observations interpolates inside the widest populated bucket and returns its upper edge, which on 2026-07-29 read 15s for a backend whose mean was 0.87s. The alert guards against this with a minimum observation rate; this panel does not.

panels.title: Request rate by model and status
panels.description: requested_model is the client-facing ALIAS, not the models[] entry name the engine panels above group by. The two label spaces do not join.

panels.title: Failures by exception
panels.description: All failures including 4xx, unlike the stat and the alert. A steady 401/403 line is a client holding a wrong or out-of-scope key: worth seeing, not worth paging on.

panels.title: End-to-end latency percentiles
panels.description: Includes generation time, so a thinking model asked for many tokens is legitimately slow. That is why nothing alerts on this panel: no single threshold is meaningful across both flavours.

panels.title: Time to first token (streaming only)
panels.description: The metric llama.cpp cannot provide. Measured baseline on four idle backends, 2026-07-29: 0.24s to 0.45s. Each engine has one KV slot, so a queued request raises this without anything being broken.

panels.title: Gateway overhead
panels.description: Time spent in the gateway rather than the engine, which is what says whether routing is free. This family names the routing group model_group and has no model label at all.

panels.title: Queue time
panels.description: Shown but deliberately not alerted on: what LiteLLM counts as queue time here has not been established against the image, and an alert on guessed semantics is worse than none. The engine-side signal is llamacpp:requests_deferred above.

panels.title: Inter-token latency by backend
panels.description: Per output token, per backend. The engine's tokens-per-second panels above are the better measure of decode speed; this one earns its place by being attributed per deployment.

panels.title: Token volume through the gateway
panels.description: The gateway's count, which is per request and attributable to a key. The engine's token counters above remain the authority on what the model actually processed.

panels.title: Requests by key
panels.description: api_key_alias is the only time-series view of which client drives load: the spend database records cost per key, not a rate. "None" is the master key, which no client should still be holding once scoped virtual keys exist.
